•  Water holding capacity (WHC): Ability of food components, especially proteins, to hold water

  •  Water activity (aw): The ratio of vapor pressure of water in food to that of pure water at the same

questions.question: Discuss the determination of Michaelis constant (Km) and Vmax.
questions.solution_html:
• The Michaelis–Menten equation describes the rate of enzyme-catalyzed reactions
  • V= Vmax/ Km+
  • Significance of Km and Vmax
  •  Km measures the affinity of the enzyme for its substrate
  • o Low Km → High affinity (enzyme binds substrate tightly)
  • o High Km → Low affinity
  •  Vmax represents the maximum rate achieved by the system when all enzyme active sites are occupied.
  • Experimental Determination
  • To determine Km and Vmax, the reaction rate is measured at various substrate concentrations.
  •  Prepare several reaction mixtures with constant enzyme concentration but varying substrate
  • concentrations.
  •  Measure the initial reaction velocity (V₀) for each substrate concentration.
  •  Plot the data to determine Km and Vmax.
  • Graphical Methods- explain graph briefly

questions.question: Explain how RM value helps in detecting adulteration in butter.
questions.solution_html:
•  RM value stands for Reichert–Meissl value.
  •  It measures the amount of volatile, water-soluble fatty acids (mainly butyric and caproic acids) in fat.
  •  It is expressed as the millilitres of 0.1 N KOH required to neutralize these acids from 5 g of fat.
  •  Pure butter fat has a high RM value (around 24–32).
  •  This is because butter contains short-chain fatty acids like butyric acid, which are volatile.
  •  Vegetable oils and animal body fats have very low RM values because they lack these volatile acids.
  •  When butter is adulterated with cheaper fats or oils, the RM value decreases.
  •  Therefore, a low RM value indicates adulteration, while a normal value shows purity.
  •  RM value is an important quality control test used in food analysis.
  •  It helps ensure consumer safety and authenticity of butter and ghee products.
questions.final_answer:  It helps ensure consumer safety and authenticity of butter and ghee products
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the structure, composition, properties and industrial uses of / starch and pectin.
questions.solution_html:
• Structure and Composition of Starch
  •  Starch is a polysaccharide made up of glucose units linked by α-glycosidic bonds.
  •  It occurs naturally in plant storage organs like cereals, potatoes, and roots.
  •  It has two main components
  •  Amylose (20–30%) – linear chain of glucose molecules.
  •  Amylopectin (70–80%) – branched chain of glucose units.
  •  The ratio of amylose and amylopectin affects starch properties like gelatinization and viscosity.
  •  Starch granules are insoluble in cold water but swell and form a gel when heated.
  • . Properties of Starch
  •  Gelatinization: When starch is heated in water, granules absorb water, swell, and lose structure to form a
  • thick paste.
  •  Retrogradation: On cooling, gelatinized starch may form a gel or recrystallize, leading to firmness (as in
  • stale bread).
  •  Hydrolysis: Starch can be broken down by enzymes (amylases) or acids to produce dextrins, maltose, and
  • glucose.
  •  Starch acts as a thickening, gelling, and stabilizing agent in many foods.
  • Structure and Composition of Pectin
  •  Pectin is a complex polysaccharide mainly composed of galacturonic acid units found in the cell walls
  • of fruits.
  •  It can form gels in the presence of sugar and acid, which makes it important in jam and jelly making.
  • Industrial Uses
  • Starch Uses
  •  Used as a thickener in soups, sauces, and gravies.
  •  Acts as a binder and filler in tablets (pharmaceutical industry).
  •  Used in textile and paper industries for sizing and coating.
  • Pectin Uses
  •  Used as a gelling agent in jams, jellies, and marmalades.
  •  Used in low-calorie foods as a fat replacer.
  •  Acts as a stabilizer in fruit juices and dairy products.
questions.final_answer:  Acts as a stabilizer in fruit juices and dairy products
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

  •  Starch granules are insoluble in cold water but swell and form a gel when heated.
  • . Properties of Starch
  •  Gelatinization: When starch is heated in water, granules absorb water, swell, and lose structure to form a
  • thick paste.
  •  Retrogradation: On cooling, gelatinized starch may form a gel or recrystallize, leading to firmness (as in
  • stale bread).
  •  Hydrolysis: Starch can be broken down by enzymes (amylases) or acids to produce dextrins, maltose, and
  • glucose.
  •  Starch acts as a thickening, gelling, and stabilizing agent in many foods.
  • Structure and Composition of Pectin
  •  Pectin is a complex polysaccharide mainly composed of galacturonic acid units found in the cell walls
  • of fruits.
  •  It can form gels in the presence of sugar and acid, which makes it important in jam and jelly making.
  • Industrial Uses
  • Starch Uses
  •  Used as a thickener in soups, sauces, and gravies.
  •  Acts as a binder and filler in tablets (pharmaceutical industry).
  •  Used in textile and paper industries for sizing and coating.
  • Pectin Uses
  •  Used as a gelling agent in jams, jellies, and marmalades.
  •  Used in low-calorie foods as a fat replacer.
  •  Acts as a stabilizer in fruit juices and dairy products.
questions.final_answer:  Acts as a stabilizer in fruit juices and dairy products
